articles.title: Florida rebuilt a degraded offshore oyster reef with dolomite limestone in 2018; within six months live-oyster density rose from near zero to 91 per square metre, and by year five it had reached 244
articles.summary: Florida’s Lone Cabbage Reef, once a productive oyster habitat that had deteriorated into a sandbar, began recovering after researchers and local oyster
articles.body: Florida’s Lone Cabbage Reef, once a productive oyster habitat that had deteriorated into a sandbar, began recovering after researchers and local oyster harvesters rebuilt it with dolomite limestone in 2018. According to the University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS), the restoration created a suitable surface for oyster larvae to settle and grow. A research study published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries subsequently documented the scale of that recovery, with live-oyster density at fixed restored offshore stations rising from near zero to 91 per square metre within six months and reaching 244 by the fifth year. The findings show how rebuilding lost reef structure can help revive a damaged marine ecosystem, although restoration alone cannot reverse every cause of oyster decline.How Florida’s oyster reef deterioratedLone Cabbage Reef lies near the mouth of the East Pass of the Suwannee River in Suwannee Sound, along Florida’s Gulf Coast. Historically, it supported oyster populations, provided habitat for fish and wildlife, and helped reduce wave action along the shoreline. Over roughly three decades, however, oyster numbers declined until the once-thriving reef collapsed and became a sandbar. The loss mattered beyond the oysters themselves. Healthy oyster reefs provide habitat for other marine life, support fisheries and help protect coastal areas from waves.Researchers spent more than a decade investigating the problem and testing possible restoration methods. Field assessments and smaller experiments conducted between 2010 and 2017 suggested that the reef’s recovery was being limited by the lack of suitable hard surfaces, rather than a shortage of oyster larvae. That distinction shaped the restoration strategy: instead of relying on oysters to return to the degraded seabed on their own, the project rebuilt the physical structure they needed to settle and grow.Why researchers chose dolomite limestoneThe large-scale restoration was completed in the summer of 2018 with support from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. The project brought together University of Florida researchers, local contractors, quarry operators and members of the Cedar Key Oystermen’s Association. The team placed locally sourced dolomite limestone across the footprint of the degraded reef. Rocks measuring between six and 36 inches were used to recreate the uneven structure of a natural oyster reef. The restored surface was also built to an elevation of about 15 to 18 inches, similar to nearby healthy reefs.This design was important because oyster larvae, known as spat, need a firm surface on which to attach and grow. The gaps between rocks also provided places for young oysters to settle. The approach produced early results. According to UF/IFAS, oyster larvae appeared within a few months of construction, and monitoring showed that the restored reef’s oyster population increased annually during the five years following restoration.Oyster density increased over five yearsThe research paper, Restoration is a partial but not complete solution for long-term declines in oyster populations: A case history from the northeastern Gulf of America, examined the reef’s recovery through repeated monitoring and comparisons between restored and unrestored areas. At four fixed restored offshore monitoring stations, mean live-oyster density increased from near zero to 91 oysters per square metre within six months. By the fifth year, it had reached 244 oysters per square metre.The study also examined the wider reef landscape. Across restored offshore sites and post-restoration monitoring periods, average oyster density was approximately 83 oysters per square metre. Model-based estimates for restored offshore reefs reached 218 oysters per square metre during the final sampling period. These figures describe different measurements: the 244 figure comes from fixed monitoring stations, while the 218 figure represents a model-based estimate at the broader landscape scale.Unrestored reefs did not show the same consistent recovery. Depending on their distance from shore, oyster densities at these sites either remained broadly stable or declined during the same period. The researchers concluded that restoring the underlying reef structure helped re-establish the conditions oysters needed to survive and grow. Fishing activity and river discharge also mattered to the wider ecosystem, but their associations with oyster density were weaker and less consistent once restoration was considered.Benefits for wildlife and local oyster harvestersThe recovery had practical implications for the local fishing community. UF/IFAS reported that oyster sizes at restored and unrestored sites had become similar within three years of the work. In the portion of the restored reef open to commercial harvesting, local oyster harvesters began finding legally sized oysters on and near the reef in 2022.Estimates indicated that the work generated $5.08 million in total industry output, including $3.02 million in regional value added, and supported 44 full-time and part-time jobs with $1.01 million in labour income. However, the results do not mean that rebuilding one reef can solve Florida’s wider oyster losses. UF/IFAS estimates that the Lone Cabbage restoration replaced only about 3% to 4% of the oyster reef area lost across the Big Bend region. Monitoring also found no evidence that the restoration changed salinity patterns in Suwannee Sound, based on measurements collected at six locations over more than five years.What the restoration means for Florida’s coastThe Lone Cabbage project demonstrates that large-scale oyster reef restoration can produce sustained improvements when the underlying habitat is rebuilt appropriately. It also highlights the value of combining scientific research with the knowledge of people who depend on the ecosystem for their livelihoods. The researchers caution, however, that restoration is only part of the solution. The causes of widespread oyster declines in the region remain incompletely understood, and the loss of reefs must be addressed on a much larger scale. The central lesson is that providing suitable limestone substrate can help oysters return to a degraded reef, but lasting recovery will also require understanding why oyster populations declined in the first place and protecting the remaining reef habitats.

articles.title: Scientists planted 40,000 native seedlings in Yosemite's damaged Tuolumne Meadows; three years later, soil organic matter was improving, but the meadow was still losing more carbon than it gained
articles.summary: Scientists who planted 40,000 native sedge seedling to restore the damaged Tuolumne Meadows in California's Yosemite National Park, have found early signs
articles.body: Scientists who planted 40,000 native sedge seedling to restore the damaged Tuolumne Meadows in California's Yosemite National Park, have found early signs of improvement after. The results, however, also show that restoring the meadow's soil and its ability to store carbon could take several decades. Three years after the planting, while the soil organic matter increased, the meadow continued to lose more carbon than it gained.The restoration project, led by researchers at Colorado State University (CSU), aims to reverse damage caused by livestock grazing more than a century ago. According to the an official release by the University, sheep grazing during the 19th century severely reduced the native plants that once covered the wet meadows. Although grazing ended long ago, the original vegetation has not returned naturally.The loss of plants has affected the soil's ability to retain moisture and store carbon. As the soil dries and organic matter continues to decompose, carbon is released from the meadow. Researchers are now trying to restore the deep-rooted vegetation that previously helped maintain these conditions.The findings, published on Tuesdat, in the Journal of Geophysical Research, Biogeosciences, suggest that the restoration is making progress, although the meadow remains degraded. Scientists believe that bringing back native sedges could help prevent further damage, but full recovery may take between 25 and 50 years.Sheep grazing damaged meadowsThe damage to Tuolumne Meadows dates back to the mid-1800s, when large numbers of livestock, mainly sheep, grazed across the landscape. Grazing continued until years after Yosemite National Park was established in 1890.During this period, sheep heavily grazed the native sedges and help store carbon in the soil. These plants were once dominant in the wet meadow ecosystem. However, their numbers declined so sharply that they have not recovered naturally, even more than a century after grazing stopped.As the sedges disappeared, shallow-rooted plants came in their place. Unlike the original vegetation, they did not provide deep-rooted biomass that helped maintain soil conditions.With time, parts of the meadow became exposed and the soil began losing moisture. According to the researchers, more than 20% of the meadow's topsoil remains bare.The deterioration has affected Yosemite's wildlife and threatened the mountain meadow landscape visited by people.Scientists planted 40,000 seedlingsTo address the damage, researchers planted 40,000 native sedge seedlings across the affected meadow and monitored changes over three years. This was done in order to reintroduce the vegetation that historically dominated the area.The results of the research showed that the planted sedges were gradually increasing soil organic matter which was encouraging because organic matter plays an important role in maintaining healthy soil.However, the improvement was not enough to reverse the meadow's overall carbon losses. The researchers also found that decomposition of existing soil organic matter was had continued. This meant the meadow was still releasing more carbon than it gained.Restoring vegetation therefore is an important first step, but rebuilding the soil's capacity to retain moisture and store carbon will require much more time.Meadow is still losing carbonThe researchers identified the loss of deep-rooted vegetation as a major reason for the meadow's continuing deterioration.Native sedges previously helped maintain soil moisture and contributed carbon to the soil. When grazing removed these plants, the meadow lost an important part of the system that supported its soil health.Without sufficient deep-rooted vegetation, the soil became drier. Continued decomposition of soil organic matter also contributed to carbon losses.The restoration project is intended to reverse these changes by re-establishing the plants that once supported the meadow's ecosystem.But the three-year results indicate that improvements in soil organic matter do not immediately mean that the meadow has regained its ability to store more carbon than it releases.Recovery could take 25 to 50 yearsDavid Cooper, the study's lead author and a senior research scientist emeritus in CSU's Department of Forest and Rangeland Stewardship, said damaged ecosystems do not always recover naturally, even when vegetation is visible."Many ecosystems do not naturally recover from severe disturbance, and while a place may look green, it may be severely degraded and in need of restoration,” Cooper said.“We feel our approach of planting the species that was and should be the dominant vegetation is the path forward.”According to Cooper, reversing damage that has developed over roughly 150 years could take another 25 to 50 years. “I think the meadow can be restored, but these things take time,” he said.

articles.title: US scientists are testing drones to find hidden Burmese pythons across the Everglades; airborne radio-tracking could make surveys faster and safer
articles.summary: A drone may help scientists find Burmese pythons hidden across the Everglades.
articles.body: A drone may help scientists find Burmese pythons hidden across the Everglades. US Geological Survey researchers are testing radio-tracking technology carried by small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS) to locate the invasive snakes more efficiently. The work aims to give researchers a clearer picture of how pythons move through the Greater Everglades Ecosystem, where their camouflage and elusive behaviour make them difficult to track.Researchers have implanted radio transmitters in some pythons to track their movements during both breeding and non-breeding seasons. According to the US Geological Survey, the airborne system is being tested to locate pythons more often, which could improve research data and efficiency while also improving staff safety.How are scientists testing drones to track hidden Burmese pythonsUSGS researchers are testing radio-tracking technology carried by sUAS, to locate Burmese pythons more efficiently. USGS is working with partners in South Florida, including the South Florida Water Management District and the UF Croc Docs Team, on a parallel study of python movement at the Francis S. Taylor Wildlife Management Area, a very different, aquatic environment. The drone testing is described as part of this movement research. Separately, researchers use location data from snakes implanted with radio-transmitters through the scout programme in Big Cypress National Preserve to study how pythons use space.The airborne system is designed to make it possible to locate tagged pythons more often while improving research data, efficiency, and staff safety during surveys.What can radio-tracking reveal about Burmese pythonsBurmese pythons are a highly cryptic species, and their movement and dispersal patterns are not well understood. Scientists at the USGS Fort Collins Science Center and Wetland and Aquatic Research Center use radio-transmitter data from scout snakes to study how pythons use space during breeding and non-breeding seasons.The information can help researchers estimate home range sizes and examine overlap in space use over long periods. It also shows how often pythons stay in the same area or move to a new one.These patterns provide information about habitat preferences and requirements, the rate at which pythons may be expanding their range, and how habitat use overlaps among pythons. The new airborne tracking system is being tested alongside this ongoing research effort.Challenge of tracking Burmese pythonsThe study forms part of a broader USGS effort to understand Burmese pythons across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem. The invasive snakes have become established across the ecosystem and pose a serious threat to native wildlife. They can reach more than 17 feet in length, while their camouflage and elusive behaviour have made them notoriously difficult to study.For over a decade, scientists and land managers have worked to understand python ecology, yet reliable population estimates have not yet been derived. USGS researchers and partners are collecting information on survival, reproduction, spatial use, feeding rates, and abundance.The research includes a year-round scout programme, in which male and female pythons are tracked continuously by researchers and University of Florida interns.How could airborne tracking support python managementThe airborne radio-tracking work is one part of research intended to provide information for managing the invasive species. USGS says its researchers are pursuing a multi-faceted strategy and working with multiple entities so data, knowledge, and resources can be shared.The broader research includes studies of vital rates, reproductive ecology, movement, deer consumption, population abundance, and mercury levels. Data from radio-tagged snakes can help researchers understand movement across different habitats and seasons.The airborne system is being tested because locating pythons more frequently may improve the information available to scientists. USGS states that if the technology proves feasible in the complex habitats of the Everglades, the innovation could strengthen invasive species management and advance restoration efforts across the Greater Everglades.

articles.title: California restored former grazing land at Dutch Slough into tidal marsh; between 2020 and 2025 Marsh Wren density jumped from 0.15 to 18.47 birds per hectare, an increase of more than 12,000%
articles.summary: California’s efforts to restore wetlands in the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta are showing measurable benefits for marsh-dwelling birds, with a newly
articles.body: California’s efforts to restore wetlands in the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta are showing measurable benefits for marsh-dwelling birds, with a newly published study documenting a dramatic rise in Marsh Wren numbers after tidal flows were reintroduced to former agricultural land. According to the journal Restoration Ecology on June 8, 2026, the research by Jason Riggio and colleagues tracked bird populations from 2020 to 2025 at restoration sites managed by the California Department of Water Resources (DWR). The findings build on the state agency’s Dutch Slough Tidal Marsh Restoration Project, which converted former grazing and dairy land into freshwater wetland habitat. The study found that Marsh Wren density at Dutch Slough rose from 0.15 birds per hectare in 2020 to 18.47 in 2025, an increase of more than 12,000%. Other marsh-associated species, including Song Sparrows and Common Yellowthroats, also recorded substantial gains as vegetation developed and the restored landscape became more suitable for wetland wildlife.How wetland restoration changed the landscapeThe Dutch Slough project is located near Oakley, at the western edge of California’s Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta. According to the DWR, the site covers 1,187 acres of former grazing and dairy land acquired as part of broader efforts to protect water quality and restore habitat in the Delta.The first phase of restoration involved reshaping the land to suitable tidal elevations, planting native vegetation and opening sections of the site to natural tidal exchange. The agency reported in November 2021 that more than half of the property had been restored, with the completed phase allowing daily tides to flow through the wetland.The work included planting more than 40,000 trees, shrubs, flowering plants and grasses, alongside approximately 25,000 tule plugs. These plants helped establish the vegetation needed to support a range of wetland species. The project was designed to deliver several benefits beyond wildlife habitat, including helping reverse land subsidence, improving environmental conditions and providing a buffer against flooding. It also serves as a living laboratory for scientists studying how restored freshwater tidal wetlands develop over time.Marsh birds responded within a few yearsThe research team analysed 1,258 bird surveys conducted between 2020 and 2025 across 26 sites at Dutch Slough, Sherman Island and Twitchell Island. The sites included restored tidal wetlands, managed freshwater marshes and unrestored pastureland, allowing researchers to compare bird communities under different habitat conditions.The results showed that several marsh-dependent species colonised the restored wetland quickly. Marsh Wren numbers rose sharply, while Song Sparrow density increased from 5.09 to 16.37 birds per hectare and Common Yellowthroat density climbed from 0.77 to 5.08 per hectare between 2020 and 2025.American Bitterns, which were not detected in the restored tidal marsh in 2020, reached an estimated density of 0.86 birds per hectare by 2025. Pied-billed Grebe density also increased, from 0.10 to 0.47 birds per hectare. These changes suggest that tidal reconnection and the development of emergent vegetation created suitable nesting and feeding conditions for species associated with freshwater marshes. Within one to four years, several marsh specialists reached densities comparable to or higher than those in established managed wetlands.Restoration also changed which birds thrivedNot every species benefited equally. As vegetation spread across the restored marsh, birds that favour open water and exposed ground became less common. Black-necked Stilt density fell from 2.47 birds per hectare in 2020 to none detected in 2025, while Killdeer numbers dropped from 1.55 to 0.10 per hectare. Mallard density also declined by 83%.The pattern reflects a natural shift in habitat as wetlands mature. Open-water areas and exposed mud can attract waterfowl and shorebirds during the early stages of restoration, while growing stands of marsh vegetation create more suitable conditions for species that nest and forage among dense plants.The research also found that restored tidal marsh supported a greater variety of waterbird species than managed marshes or pastureland. By 2025, tidal marsh sites averaged seven waterbird species, compared with 3.8 in managed marshes and 1.8 in pastureland. However, overall bird species richness remained relatively stable throughout the study period. The findings suggest that restoration changed the composition of bird communities rather than simply increasing the total number of species present.Why the findings matter for future restorationThe Dutch Slough project demonstrates how restoring natural water movement can help re-establish wildlife habitat in a heavily modified landscape. The Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta has undergone extensive changes through agricultural development, land drainage and the construction of levees, leaving much of its original wetland ecosystem altered.According to the researchers, continued monitoring will be important to establish whether the early gains persist as vegetation matures. Maintaining different habitat types across the wider landscape could also help support species with contrasting needs, including birds that depend on open water and exposed ground. The study, published in Restoration Ecology, adds evidence that large-scale wetland restoration can produce measurable ecological benefits within a relatively short period. At Dutch Slough, the sharp rise in Marsh Wren density offers one of the clearest examples of how wildlife can respond when a landscape is reconnected to its natural tidal processes.

articles.title: US wildlife partners spent years protecting more than 1,700 acres along Wisconsin's Lake Superior shore; the project has restored wetlands, treated invasive plants and reconnected cold-water habitat
articles.summary: A multi-year conservation project along Wisconsin’s Lake Superior shoreline has helped protect more than 1,700 acres of land, restore wetlands and improve
articles.body: A multi-year conservation project along Wisconsin’s Lake Superior shoreline has helped protect more than 1,700 acres of land, restore wetlands and improve habitats used by fish, migratory birds and other wildlife. The project brought together the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and Landmark Conservancy, a nonprofit organisation based in Menomonie, Wisconsin. Supported by federal funding and the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, the effort focused on protecting connected natural areas along Lake Superior’s southern shore. As reported by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the conservation work was aimed at maintaining healthy forests, wetlands and streams while protecting the watersheds that feed into Lake Superior.Why the Lake Superior shoreline mattersIn northern Wisconsin, rivers and streams flow into Lake Superior through a landscape of forests, wetlands and cold-water tributaries. These connected habitats support brook trout, migratory birds and other wildlife, while helping maintain the health of the wider Great Lakes ecosystem. The region is known to biologists as the south shore streams area. Protecting it is important because the condition of the land surrounding rivers and streams affects the habitats and waters they support. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Landmark Conservancy worked with willing landowners to identify conservation opportunities in the watersheds of Whittlesey Creek, Iron River, Marengo River, Pokegama River and White River.The project used conservation easements as one of its main tools. These agreements can help protect land from certain types of future development while allowing owners to retain ownership, depending on the terms of the agreement. They also help conservation groups safeguard connected habitats across different properties.Wetlands restored and 25 acres treated for invasive speciesThe project involved more than protecting land. Landmark Conservancy also carried out restoration work in community forests in northern Wisconsin. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the work included planting conifers in forested wetlands, using native plants to restore habitat and treating 25 acres for invasive species. Invasive plants can spread into natural areas and compete with native vegetation, changing the conditions on which local wildlife depends. Treating affected areas can help native plant communities recover and improve the quality of the surrounding habitat.Planting conifers in forested wetlands and restoring areas with native vegetation were also intended to support the landscape’s long-term health. The conservation work covered more than 1,700 acres, but the agency’s report does not describe all of that area as newly restored. It refers to conservation actions across the land, alongside specific restoration and invasive-species management activities.A partnership involving landowners and conservation groupsThe US Fish and Wildlife Service’s Coastal Program supported Landmark Conservancy’s multi-year project. Local landowners played an important role by working with the organisation to identify areas where conservation measures could be introduced. The partnership also focused on explaining local conservation needs and helping landowners understand how protecting natural areas can improve the long-term resilience of the Great Lakes region.The project was selected as part of the broader goals of the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative’s Action Plan IV. It described the work as an example of how federal financial support, local expertise and voluntary conservation can work together. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative is led by the US Environmental Protection Agency and involves more than a dozen federal agencies, including the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Its work addresses major environmental concerns affecting the Great Lakes.What happens next?The protected areas are expected to continue providing habitat for wildlife, maintaining links between natural areas and supporting the health of local watersheds. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the relationships built between landowners and conservation partners could also create opportunities for future conservation work. The project is part of a broader effort to protect the Great Lakes, which support wildlife as well as communities that depend on the region for drinking water and recreation.

articles.title: Scientists examined a 165-million-year-old fossil from China and found a broad swimming tail plus bony throat structures; the Jurassic mammal predecessor could feed and swallow in ways seen in modern mammals
articles.summary: Scientists have examined a 165-million-year-old fossil found in China and identified a mammal predecessor that had a broad tail for swimming and throat
articles.body: Scientists have examined a 165-million-year-old fossil found in China and identified a mammal predecessor that had a broad tail for swimming and throat bones similar to those found in modern mammals. The discovery suggests that some early relatives of mammals had already developed ways of chewing and swallowing food millions of years before modern mammals evolved.The newly identified species, named Megacauda sungei, lived during the Jurassic period. Researchers from the University of Chicago studied its well-preserved fossil and found that the animal had strong hind limbs, a flattened tail and specialised throat structures. Their findings were published in the journal Natureon on Wednesday.The animal belonged to an extinct group called docodonts, which were close relatives of mammals during the Mesozoic Era. It measured around 40 to 50 centimetres in length and weighed between one and two kilograms. Its physical features suggest that it spent time both on land and in water, much like modern semi-aquatic mammals.What makes the discovery important is the combination of its swimming adaptations and feeding structures. The fossil contains delicate bones that helped support muscles involved in swallowing. According to researchers, these structures provide some of the earliest evidence of a feeding mechanism that later became important in the evolution of mammals with different diets.Ancient animal swallowed like modern mammalsOne of the most important findings concerns the hyoid bones, which help connect the mouth and throat in mammals. In modern mammals, including humans, these bones form part of a structure that supports the muscles used during swallowing.The bones are arranged in a U-shaped structure and connected to the skull through smaller bony segments. This arrangement allows mammals to chew their food and then swallow it in smaller portions, rather than swallowing large pieces or entire prey as animals such as alligators do. These structures also play a role in allowing young mammals to suckle their mother's milk.Researchers found that Megacaudahad similar structures beneath its skull. The preservation was detailed enough for scientists to examine the arrangement of the bones and understand how they supported the muscles involved in feeding.Zhe-Xi Luo, professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study, explained why this development mattered.“This is an incredibly important evolutionary innovation. After mammals chew their food, be it plants or meat, they all swallow it in the same efficient and effortless way,” Luo said.“Once early mammals had this apparatus, each group could develop specialized teeth and diversify into a tremendous range of food resources. They could be carnivores, insectivores, herbivores, omnivores, or anywhere in between.”According to study co-author Peishu Li, the animal's throat anatomy can be compared with the throat muscles of the modern opossum.How Megacauda moved through waterApart from its throat structures, the fossil also provided evidence of how the animal moved and hunted. Its hind limbs had long outer digits similar to those of a platypus. The tail contained wide, H-shaped vertebrae and had a broad outline that would have helped propel the animal through water.The skull also contained strong canine teeth and sharp cheek teeth capable of cutting and chewing meat. However, the arrangement of these teeth differed from those of modern carnivorous mammals.Researchers also found tiny pieces of vertebrate bones preserved in the animal's stomach. This suggests that it fed on small animals, possibly including salamanders, whose fossils have also been found in the same geological deposits.Based on these features, scientists believe Megacaudafollowed a semi-aquatic lifestyle, entering water to hunt while also spending time on land.The discovery adds to earlier evidence that docodonts occupied different habitats. In 2006, Luo's team identified another swimming docodont called Castorocauda. The newly studied Megacaudafossil is older and preserves more of the skeleton.“The new fossil is particularly interesting because it’s older than Castorocauda. Although both docodonts occupied the same niche in the water, the new fossil is more complete,” said April I. Neander, a scientific artist and CT imaging specialist at the University of Chicago.How scientists examined fossilThe fossil was discovered in China's Inner Mongolia region. During the COVID-19 pandemic, study co-author Chang-Fu Zhou from Shandong University of Science and Technology transported the specimen to different research laboratories for examination.Scientists used CT scanning and X-ray fluorescence photography to study the fossil. Because the original slab was large, it had to be divided into smaller pieces before scanning. Neander then used the scans to reconstruct and examine the preserved anatomical structures in detail.The researchers also compared the specimen with Microdocodon gracilis, a much smaller docodont identified by Luo and colleagues in 2019. That animal, which lived around the same geological period, also possessed mammal-like hyoid bones.The new fossil provides further evidence that complex throat structures had already appeared among early mammal relatives during the Jurassic period.Luo said the nearly complete specimen also helps researchers understand how these animals lived in ecosystems dominated by dinosaurs.The findings suggest that important changes in swallowing and feeding anatomy were taking place long before modern mammals separated from their evolutionary predecessors. These developments later helped mammals evolve specialised teeth and adapt to a wide range of food sources.
